questions.official_guidance: To avoid the possibility of selection of the reported result, finalization of the analysis intentions must precede availability of unblinded outcome data to the trial investigators. Changes to analysis plans that were made before unblinded outcome data were available, or that were clearly unrelated to the results, do not raise concerns about bias in selection of the reported result.

questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish protocol or ethics approval, plan finalization, amendment effective dates, registry posting or update, data cutoff, database lock, and investigators' access to unblinded outcome data; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis. Capture each dated event as reported; approval, cutoff, or database lock does not by itself establish when investigators could see unblinded outcomes.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An SAP embedded in a protocol, supplement, or combined document is still plan Evidence when its section and scope can be located; a separate SAP file is not required. An absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
The result did not follow such a pre-specified plan.
Analysis intentions or their timing are not sufficiently reported.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data. Protocol approval, ethics approval, amendment, initial registry posting, registry update, retrieval, data cutoff, and database lock are distinct events; none substitutes for the source-located date of plan finalization or investigator access to unblinded results.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent. A data cutoff or database lock is not itself proof of when investigators accessed unblinded outcomes. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results. Not establishing that a plan was early is not evidence that it was late: ground a negative chronology inference in source facts and trial circumstances, or preserve no_information when those cannot support a reasonable probable answer.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; a source-located finalization date before investigator access differs from the same plan with access timing unresolved.

A plan may be an identified section of a combined protocol or supplement. Navigate to that section and retain its exact Source and page coordinates; the lack of a separately named SAP file does not show that no plan exists.

Distinguish confidential data-monitoring access from access by trial investigators making analysis decisions. Staff providing confidential data to a monitoring committee are excepted in the official guidance; that access alone does not establish late prespecification. Public interim results are different evidence. Refining an analysis with blinded data is generally acceptable unless variables reveal intervention identity.

All the patients except those who crossed over un- derwent surgery within 2 months after random- ization; the median time between randomization and surgery was 23 days (interquartile range, 10 to 36). There was no operative mortality in the early- surgery group. Of the 72 patients assigned to conservative care, 53 patients (74%) underwent surgical aortic-valve replacement (52 patients) or transcatheter aortic- valve replacement (TAVR) (1 patient) during fol- low-up, mainly because of the development of symptoms (in 43 patients). Indications for aortic- valve replacement are listed in Table S2. Among these 53 patients, urgent surgery was performed in 9 patients (17%) who were admitted from the emergency department. There was no operative mortality among the patients who later underwent aortic-valve replacement; the median time from randomization to aortic-valve replacement was 700 days (interquartile range, 277 to 1469). Ad- ditional information on surgical procedures and results are provided in Table S3 and the Supple- mental Surgical Results section in the Supplemen- tary Appendix. Follow-up and End Points Data collection ended in April 2019, when the last enrolled patient had completed 4 years of follow- up. The median follow-up was 6.2 years (interquar- tile range, 5.0 to 7.4) in the early-surgery group and 6.1 years (interquartile range, 4.5 to 7.3) in the conservative-care group. No patients were lost to follow-up. In an intention-to-treat analysis including all the trial patients, 1 of 73 patients assigned to early surgery (1%) and 11 of 72 patients assigned to conservative care (15%) died from cardiovascu- lar causes (hazard ratio, 0.09; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.01 to 0.67) (Table 2). guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.

A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer. For D3.2 No, inspected context/inference or a valid scoped no-hit receipt can instead support the scoped absence of reassuring evidence; it does not assert bias occurred.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and uncertainty in inspected Evidence, scoped search receipts, or an explicit scientific limitation. Complete reading_recovery with read_pages and all context continuations. Document-structure recovery in coverage is navigation, not selected Evidence; inspect relevant unopened windows before claiming information is unreported, or retain a bounded stopping rationale. Inactive extras are ignored.

38|BACKGROUND
39|The timing and indications for surgical intervention in asymptomatic patients with
40|severe aortic stenosis remain controversial.
41|METHODS
42|In a multicenter trial, we randomly assigned 145 asymptomatic patients with very
43|severe aortic stenosis (defined as an aortic-valve area of ≤0.75 cm2 with either an
44|aortic jet velocity of ≥4.5 m per second or a mean transaortic gradient of ≥50 mm Hg)
45|to early surgery or to conservative care according to the recommendations of cur-
46|rent guidelines. The primary end point was a composite of death during or within
47|30 days after surgery (often called operative mortality) or death from cardiovascular
48|causes during the entire follow-up period. The major secondary end point was death
49|from any cause during follow-up.
50|RESULTS
51|In the early-surgery group, 69 of 73 patients (95%) underwent surgery within 2 months
52|after randomization, and there was no operative mortality. In an intention-to-treat
53|analysis, a primary end-point event occurred in 1 patient in the early-surgery group
54|(1%) and in 11 of 72 patients in the conservative-care group (15%) (hazard ratio,
55|0.09; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.01 to 0.67; P = 0.003). Death from any cause
56|occurred in 5 patients in the early-surgery group (7%) and in 15 patients in the con-
57|servative-care group (21%) (hazard ratio, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.90). In the con-
58|servative-care group, the cumulative incidence of sudden death was 4% at 4 years
59|and 14% at 8 years.
60|CONCLUSIONS
61|Among asymptomatic patients with very severe aortic stenosis, the incidence of the
62|composite of operative mortality or death from cardiovascular causes during the
63|follow-up period was significantly lower among those who underwent early aortic-
64|valve replacement surgery than among those who received conservative care. (Fund-
65|ed by the Korean Institute of Medicine; RECOVERY ClinicalTrials.gov number,
66|NCT01161732.)

5|ortic stenosis is the most common
6|valvular disease for which surgery is in-
7|dicated in developed countries, and the
8|prevalence of this condition is increasing because
9|of the aging population.1 Aortic-valve replacement
10|is the only effective therapy for severe symptom-
11|atic aortic stenosis, and despite limited data from
12|randomized clinical trials, current guidelines rec-
13|ommend aortic-valve replacement because of the
14|dismal natural history of this disorder.1,2 Although
15|one third to one half of patients with severe aortic
16|stenosis are asymptomatic at the time of diagno-
17|sis,3,4 appropriate timing of intervention for these
18|patients remains controversial.5,6 On the basis of
19|a consensus opinion that the potential benefit of
20|aortic-valve replacement to prevent sudden death
21|in asymptomatic patients (which has an incidence
22|of approximately 1% per year) may not be greater
23|than the risk of death during or within 30 days
24|after surgery (often called operative mortality) and
25|death related to the aortic-valve prosthesis, obser-
26|vation is recommended for the majority of asymp-
27|tomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis, and
28|aortic-valve replacement is recommended once
29|symptoms develop.1,2,4 However, advances in sur-
30|gical techniques and aortic-valve prostheses may
31|change the risk-to-benefit ratio of aortic-valve re-
32|placement, especially among patients at low sur-
33|gical risk.7-9
34|The Randomized Comparison of Early Surgery
35|versus Conventional Treatment in Very Severe
36|Aortic Stenosis (RECOVERY) trial was designed
37|to compare long-term clinical outcomes of early
38|surgical aortic-valve replacement with those of a
39|conservative care strategy based on current guide-
40|lines in asymptomatic patients with very severe
41|aortic stenosis (transvalvular velocity ≥4.5 m per
42|second). The major hypothesis of this trial was
43|that the incidence of death from cardiovascular
44|causes would be lower among patients who under-
45|went early surgery than among those who received
46|conservative care.
47|Methods
48|Trial Design and Oversight
49|We conducted this multicenter, randomized, par-
50|allel-group, open-label trial involving asymptom-
51|atic patients with very severe aortic stenosis who
52|were candidates for either early surgery or conser-
53|vative care at four medical centers in Korea. The
54|trial protocol (available with the full text of this
55|article at NEJM.org) was designed by the principal
56|investigator and approved by the institutional re-
57|view board at each participating center. The Ko-
58|rean Institute of Medicine, which supported the
59|trial coordinators during the first 2 years of the
60|trial, had no role in the collection, analysis, or
61|interpretation of the data, writing of the manu-
62|script, or any other aspect of the trial. The trial
63|received no other external sources of funding.
64|The trial was conducted in accordance with
65|the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
66|An independent clinical-events committee ad-
67|judicated all serious adverse events, and a data
68|and safety monitoring board oversaw the safety
69|of the trial. The first draft of the manuscript
70|was prepared by the first author and was re-
71|viewed and edited by all the authors. All the
72|authors made the decision to submit the manu-
73|script for publication and vouch for the accu-
74|racy and completeness of the data and for the
75|fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
76|Patient Selection
77|We screened consecutive patients who were 20 to
78|80 years of age and who presented with very se-
79|vere aortic stenosis, which was assessed by means
80|of transthoracic echocardiography. In accordance
81|with the 1998 American College of Cardiology-
82|American Heart Association (ACC-AHA) guide-
83|lines and a traditional definition of severe aortic
84|stenosis,10,11 we defined very severe aortic steno-
85|sis as an aortic-valve area of 0.75 cm2 or less
86|with either a peak aortic jet velocity of 4.5 m per
87|second or greater or a mean transaortic gradient
88|of 50 mm Hg or greater.
89|In accordance with the 2006 ACC-AHA guide-
90|lines on surgical indications for severe aortic
91|stenosis,12 patients were excluded if they had ex-
92|ertional dyspnea, syncope, presyncope or angina,
93|a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 50%,
94|or clinically significant aortic regurgitation or
95|mitral valve disease or if they had undergone
96|cardiac surgery. Exercise testing was selectively
97|performed to evaluate patients with nonspecific
98|symptoms, and patients with a positive exercise
99|test were excluded. We also excluded patients who
100|were not candidates for early surgery because of
101|age (>80 years) or a medical condition such as
102|cancer. All the participants provided written in-
103|formed consent.

4|Trial Procedures
5|Eligibility was determined after each patient un-
6|derwent a thorough evaluation of symptoms and
7|medical records and results of echocardiography
8|and exercise testing were reviewed. Details re-
9|garding echocardiography and exercise testing are
10|provided in the Supplementary Appendix, available
11|at NEJM.org. Patients were randomly assigned in
12|a 1:1 ratio to early surgery or conservative care
13|with the use of a Web-based interactive response
14|system. The assignment to each treatment group
15|was computer-generated and stratified according
16|to the participating center by means of a permuted-
17|block sequence with variable block size.
18|The protocol specified that patients assigned
19|to the early-surgery group should undergo aortic-
20|valve replacement within 2 months after random-
21|ization. Patients assigned to the conservative-care
22|group received treatment according to the ACC-
23|AHA guidelines,2,12 and they were referred for
24|surgery if they became symptomatic during fol-
25|low-up, if the left ventricular ejection fraction
26|decreased to less than 50%, or if the peak aortic
27|jet velocity increased each year by more than 0.5 m
28|per second on follow-up echocardiography. Details
29|regarding surgical procedures and patient follow-
30|up are provided in the Supplementary Appendix.
31|Trial End Points
32|The primary end point was a composite of op-
33|erative mortality or death from cardiovascular
34|causes during the follow-up period (continuing
35|until 4 years after the last patient was enrolled).
36|Prespecified secondary end points included death
37|from any cause, repeat aortic-valve surgery, clini-
38|cal thromboembolic events, and hospitalization
39|for heart failure during follow-up. Specific defi-
40|nitions of trial end points are provided in the
41|Supplementary Appendix.
42|Statistical Analysis
43|On the basis of our previous observational study,13
44|we estimated that a sample of 144 patients would
45|provide the trial with 80% power, at a two-sided
46|significance level of 0.05, to detect a significant
47|difference with respect to the primary end point,
48|assuming that the incidence of the primary end
49|point would be 16% in the conservative-care group
50|and 2% in the early-surgery group during a follow-
51|up period that continued until 4 years after the last
52|patient was enrolled. In calculating the sample size
53|by a log-rank survival power analysis, we also
54|assumed that an enrollment period of 2 years
55|would be needed to complete enrollment and that
56|the rate of loss to follow-up would be 10%.
57|Analyses were performed on an intention-to-
58|treat basis. Differences between the treatment
59|groups were evaluated with the use of Student's
60|t-test for continuous variables and Fisher's exact
61|test for categorical variables. Because random-
62|ization was stratified according to the partici-
63|pating center, we analyzed the end points with
64|the use of stratified Cox proportional-hazards re-
65|gression with Firth correction. Estimates of cu-
66|mulative incidences were calculated by the Kaplan-
67|Meier method and were compared with the use
68|of the log-rank test. For the Kaplan-Meier analy-
69|sis, we analyzed all clinical events according to

27|Discussion
28|The RECOVERY trial compared early surgery with
29|conservative care in asymptomatic patients with
30|very severe aortic stenosis. The trial showed a
31|lower incidence of the primary end point of opera-
32|tive mortality or death from cardiovascular causes
33|during the follow-up period among patients who
34|underwent early surgery than among those who
35|received conservative care. Moreover, early surgery
36|was associated with a lower incidence of death
37|from any cause among such patients.
38|The decision to perform surgery in an asymp-
39|tomatic patient requires careful weighing of the
40|risks of early aortic-valve replacement against those
41|of observation. In patients with asymptomatic se-
42|vere aortic stenosis, it has generally appeared to
43|be relatively safe to follow a watchful waiting
44|strategy and delay surgery until symptoms de-
45|velop.14 However, this conservative care strategy
46|is also associated with a risk of sudden death,
47|denial or late reporting of symptoms by patients,
48|irreversible myocardial damage, and an increase
49|in surgical risk while waiting for symptoms to
50|develop.4-6 In previous observational studies, base-
51|line differences between the treatment groups,
52|treatment-selection bias, and unmeasured con-
53|founders might have influenced the results.13,15
54|By reducing these limitations inherent to observa-
55|tional studies,4,16 this randomized trial provides
56|evidence to support early aortic-valve replacement
57|in asymptomatic patients with very severe aortic
58|stenosis.

4|the two groups. First, surgical risk was substan-
5|tially lower in this trial and in recent trials com-
6|paring surgical aortic-valve replacement with TAVR
7|in low-risk patients8,9 than in previous studies; in
8|our trial, the incidence of operative mortality was
9|less than 1%. Close monitoring was performed
10|after surgery, and improvements in postoperative
11|care contributed to a substantial decrease in the
12|long-term risk associated with early aortic-valve
13|replacement. Second, early surgery appeared to
14|prevent sudden death, because no cases of sudden
15|death occurred in the early-surgery group. In con-
16|trast, in the conservative-care group, the annual
17|risk of sudden death tended to increase during the
18|progression of aortic stenosis before the develop-
19|ment of symptoms. Third, eventual aortic-valve
20|replacement was almost unavoidable in the con-
21|servative-care group, and the overall risk of aortic-
22|valve replacement appeared to increase while
23|surgery was deferred until symptoms developed.
24|Cardiovascular events that occurred after surgery
25|were more frequently observed in the conserva-
26|tive-care group, suggesting a higher long-term
27|risk associated with later aortic-valve replacement.
28|Our trial has several limitations. First, the
29|risk-benefit ratio may be shifted toward a benefit
30|of early surgery in this trial involving patients
31|with very severe aortic stenosis because the risk
32|of waiting increases according to the severity of
33|aortic stenosis.5 The benefit of early surgery may
34|be relatively smaller in asymptomatic patients
35|with less severe aortic stenosis. Second, crossover
36|occurred in 5% of the patients in the early-surgery
37|group and in 3% of the patients in the conserva-
38|tive-care group. Nevertheless, the results of the
39|per-protocol analysis were similar to those of the
40|primary intention-to-treat analysis. Third, since
41|this trial was not blinded, the nonfatal outcomes
42|could have been influenced by the clinician's
43|knowledge of the treatment the patient received.
44|Fourth, exercise testing is reasonable to confirm
45|the absence of symptoms in asymptomatic patients
46|with severe aortic stenosis,2 but it was performed
47|only selectively in this trial. Fifth, the small num-
48|bers of trial patients and primary end-point events
49|constitute an important limitation of this trial.
50|However, it was the judgment of the investigators
51|that a larger number of patients than the calcu-
52|lated sample size could not be enrolled for ethical
53|and logistic reasons. Finally, this trial included
54|relatively young patients (as compared with pa-
55|tients enrolled in recent TAVR trials involving low-
56|risk patients8,9), among whom the incidence of
57|bicuspid aortic-valve disease was high and who
58|had normal left ventricular systolic function, few
59|coexisting conditions, and low operative risk.
60|Thus, our trial population is quite different from
61|the populations enrolled in TAVR trials,8,9,17-19 and
62|the results of our trial cannot be directly applied
63|to early TAVR for asymptomatic severe aortic ste-
64|nosis. Because the incidence of operative mortal-
65|ity was very low in our trial, our results may not
66|be applicable to low-volume medical centers or to
67|patients at high operative risk.
68|In conclusion, in this randomized trial, early
69|surgical aortic-valve replacement resulted in a sig-
70|nificantly lower risk of operative mortality or death
71|from cardiovascular causes during the follow-up
72|period than conservative care among asymptom-
73|atic patients with very severe aortic stenosis.

Trial Procedures
Eligibility was determined after each patient un-
derwent a thorough evaluation of symptoms and
medical records and results of echocardiography
and exercise testing were reviewed. Details re-
garding echocardiography and exercise testing are
provided in the Supplementary Appendix, available
at NEJM.org. Patients were randomly assigned in
a 1:1 ratio to early surgery or conservative care
with the use of a Web-based interactive response
system. The assignment to each treatment group
was computer-generated and stratified according
to the participating center by means of a permuted-
block sequence with variable block size.
The protocol specified that patients assigned
to the early-surgery group should undergo aortic-
valve replacement within 2 months after random-
ization. Patients assigned to the conservative-care
group received treatment according to the ACC-
AHA guidelines,2,12 and they were referred for
surgery if they became symptomatic during fol-
low-up, if the left ventricular ejection fraction
decreased to less than 50%, or if the peak aortic
jet velocity increased each year by more than 0.5 m
per second on follow-up echocardiography. Details
regarding surgical procedures and patient follow-
up are provided in the Supplementary Appendix.
Trial End Points
The primary end point was a composite of op-
erative mortality or death from cardiovascular
causes during the follow-up period (continuing
until 4 years after the last patient was enrolled).
Prespecified secondary end points included death
from any cause, repeat aortic-valve surgery, clini-
cal thromboembolic events, and hospitalization
for heart failure during follow-up. Specific defi-
nitions of trial end points are provided in the
Supplementary Appendix.
Statistical Analysis
On the basis of our previous observational study,13
we estimated that a sample of 144 patients would
provide the trial with 80% power, at a two-sided
significance level of 0.05, to detect a significant
difference with respect to the primary end point,
assuming that the incidence of the primary end
point would be 16% in the conservative-care group
and 2% in the early-surgery group during a follow-
up period that continued until 4 years after the last
patient was enrolled. In calculating the sample size
by a log-rank survival power analysis, we also
assumed that an enrollment period of 2 years
would be needed to complete enrollment and that
the rate of loss to follow-up would be 10%.
Analyses were performed on an intention-to-
treat basis. Differences between the treatment
groups were evaluated with the use of Student's
t-test for continuous variables and Fisher's exact
test for categorical variables. Because random-
ization was stratified according to the partici-
pating center, we analyzed the end points with
the use of stratified Cox proportional-hazards re-
gression with Firth correction. Estimates of cu-
mulative incidences were calculated by the Kaplan-
Meier method and were compared with the use
of the log-rank test. For the Kaplan-Meier analy-
sis, we analyzed all clinical events according to
the time to the first event. Hazard ratios with
95% confidence intervals were derived with the
use of the stratified Cox proportional-hazards
model with Firth correction. The 95% confidence
intervals have not been adjusted for multiple com-
parisons, and therefore inferences drawn from
these intervals may not be reproducible.
For the primary end-point analysis, we also
performed a competing-risk analysis in which
death due to a cause other than a cardiovascular
cause was considered as a competing risk, and
hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were
calculated with the use of the method of Fine and
Gray. The cumulative incidences of the primary
end point were also compared between the treat-
ment groups with the use of Gray's test. Subgroup
analyses were performed to determine whether
the result of the primary end point was consistent
in two prespecified subgroups defined according
to peak aortic velocity and cause of aortic stenosis.
A per-protocol analysis of the primary end point
was also performed. All reported P values were
two-sided, and a P value of less than 0.05 was
considered to indicate statistical significance. We
used SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute), for
statistical analyses.

Statistical Analysis Plan

Sample Size Calculation
We tried to determine the rate of primary endpoint based on the randomized trials, but no randomized
trial has been conducted to evaluate outcomes of early surgery. Using a prospective registry data, we
recently reported that the estimated actuarial 6-year survival and cardiac mortality-free survival rates
were 98±1% and 100% in the early surgery group, 68±6% and 76±5% in the conventional treatment
group, respectively (p < 0.001) (9). Based on our prospective observational study, we estimated that a
sample size of 144 patients would provide 80% power to detect a significant difference with respect to
the primary end point at the 2-sided significance level of 0.05, assuming that the 4-year rate of a
composite end point (cardiac mortality or operative mortality) would be 16% in the conventional
treatment group and 2% in the early surgery group.

Analysis of primary and secondary end point
All primary and secondary endpoints will be analyzed on an intent-to-treat basis (all patients analyzed
as part of their assigned treatment group). For intent-to-treat analysis, all patients who sign the written
informed consent form and are randomized in the study will be included in the analysis, regardless of
whether or not the correct treatment is administered, or whether crossover occurs.
To analyze outcomes, estimates of cumulative event rates will be calculated by the Kaplan-Meier
method and compared employing the log-rank test. For Kaplan-Meier analysis, we will analyze all
